runs.text:
Tides happen because the Moon and, to a lesser extent, the Sun pull on Earth’s oceans with gravity, and because Earth is rotating. The Moon’s gravity is strongest on the side of Earth nearest it and weakest on the far side, so the ocean is pulled slightly toward the Moon on the near side and left behind on the far side. In effect, the water bulges outward on both sides of Earth, creating two high-tide regions and two low-tide regions at once. The Sun does the same thing, but its effect is smaller because it is much farther away; when the Sun and Moon line up, their pulls reinforce each other and produce especially large tides, while when they are at right angles their effects partly cancel and produce smaller tides.

As Earth rotates, a given coastline passes through these bulges, so the water level rises and falls in a regular cycle. Most places see two high tides and two low tides each day, roughly twelve hours apart, though the exact timing and height vary with location, coastline shape, water depth, and weather. Tides are not simply water “moving in and out” from one place; they are a wave-like redistribution of the whole ocean, and the Moon’s pull also affects the solid Earth slightly. In shallow bays and estuaries, the tide can be amplified, and in some places the geometry produces only one high and one low tide per day. Wind and atmospheric pressure can add or subtract a little height, but the basic rhythm of the tides comes from the gravitational tug of the Moon and Sun combined with Earth’s rotation.
